challenges.name: node-test-assertions-quiz
challenges.title: What does this assertion actually prove?
challenges.description: Two assertions from the checkout test suite. Decide what each one checks - and what it lets through.

questions.explanation: strictEqual compares with Object.is. For objects that means "is this the very same object in memory?", and a freshly created object is never the same object as the literal written in the test, even with identical contents. deepStrictEqual compares structure instead: same own keys, same values (compared strictly, so 2 and '2' differ), same prototype. Importing plain 'node:assert' changes nothing here: strictEqual always uses Object.is - only the legacy equal/deepEqual are loose there. assert.ok only checks truthiness, so it would pass for any object at all, including a wrong one.

options.text: Use assert.deepStrictEqual, which compares keys and values (and the prototype) instead of object identity.
Use assert.ok(toCartLine('A1', 2)), because the function clearly returns an object.
Import assert from 'node:assert' instead of 'node:assert/strict', so strictEqual becomes a loose comparison.
Nothing is wrong with the test: toCartLine must return the same object instance that the test created.

questions.explanation: assert.ok(value) passes for every truthy value. It proves only that applyDiscount(8000, 10) did not throw and did not return a falsy value (0, '', null, undefined, NaN, false). A price of 800 (the discount instead of the price), 8000 (no discount) or the string '7200' all pass, so it cannot tell a correct function from a broken one. Worse, it would FAIL for a correct 100% discount, whose price is 0. A useful assertion compares against an exact expected value: assert.strictEqual(applyDiscount(8000, 10), 7200).

options.text: It passes if applyDiscount returns 800 (the discount amount) instead of 7200 (the price).
It proves that the returned price is a number.
It would fail for a correct applyDiscount(8000, 100), because the right answer, 0, is falsy.
It proves the threshold works, because 8000 is above 5000.

challenges.name: tests-that-catch-bugs
challenges.title: Write tests that catch the discount bugs
challenges.description: Replace the incident's assert.ok test with a suite that actually catches bugs. The grader runs your discountSuite(applyDiscount, assert) against the correct applyDiscount - where it must pass - and against several buggy versions, where it must fail. Cover the happy path, both sides of the threshold, 0%, and invalid input on both ends of the range.

tests.name: Your suite passes against the correct applyDiscount
Catches: returns the discount amount instead of the price
Catches: a cart of exactly 5000 cents gets no discount
Catches: an explicit 0% falls back to the default 10%
Catches: a percent above 100 is accepted
Catches a bug you were not told about
